seo_title: What Is a Roofing Scope of Loss? A Texas Homeowner Guide
meta_description: What a roofing scope of loss includes, how to spot missing items like flashing and drip edge, and how to dispute an incomplete scope.
h1: What Is a Roofing Scope of Loss? How to Read and Check Yours
excerpt: A roofing scope of loss lists every roof repair item your insurer will pay for. Learn what belongs in it, what is often missing, and how Texas homeowners can fix an incomplete scope.
key_takeaways: A roofing scope of loss is the itemized list of roof work an insurer agrees to pay for.
Missing slopes, flashing, drip edge, and low waste factors are common scope gaps.
Compare the scope line by line against your contractor estimate, not just the totals.
Supplements and appraisal are the main tools for correcting an incomplete roof scope.
body_html:
A roofing scope of loss is the itemized description of the roof damage an insurance company agrees to repair or replace after a covered loss. It lists measurements, materials, labor, and accessories such as flashing and vents. If an item is missing from the roofing scope of loss, it usually is not paid.

What does a roofing scope of loss mean?

"Scope" is short for scope of work. In a roof claim, the scope of loss is the adjuster's written list of everything that must be removed, replaced, or repaired to put the roof back to its pre-loss condition. It is usually built in estimating software such as Xactimate or Symbility.

Each line in the scope has a description, a quantity, a unit (squares, linear feet, or each), and a price. Add the lines together, apply tax, overhead and profit where allowed, and subtract depreciation and your deductible, and you arrive at what the carrier pays.

The scope also becomes the baseline for everything that follows: supplement requests, recoverable depreciation, and, if the dispute continues, appraisal. A clean, complete scope early in the claim prevents months of back-and-forth later.

That is why the roofing scope of loss matters more than any single photo or inspection note. It is the document that turns damage into dollars.

What is usually included in a roofing scope of loss?

A complete scope for a shingle roof replacement typically covers the items below. Tile, metal, and low-slope roofs have their own components, but the logic is the same: every layer and every accessory needs a line.

Scope itemWhy it matters
Tear-off and disposalOld roofing must be removed and hauled away before new material goes on.
Shingles (correct type)Three-tab, laminated, and impact-resistant shingles are priced very differently.
Starter courseSecures the first row of shingles at eaves and rakes.
Ridge and hip capUsually priced separately from field shingles.
UnderlaymentThe water-resistant layer beneath the shingles; type may be dictated by code.
Drip edgeDirects water off roof edges and is required by many current codes.
Flashing (step, counter, valley, chimney)Protects every wall, chimney, and valley intersection from leaks.
Pipe jacks, vents, and bootsPenetrations are replaced or reset with the new roof.
Steep and high-roof chargesExtra labor and safety equipment on steep pitches or two-story roofs.
Permits and code itemsLocal requirements that must be met for the repair to pass inspection.

Removal and disposal

Tear-off should match the number of layers actually on the roof. A second layer of shingles adds removal labor and dumpster weight. If the scope shows one layer and your roof has two, the numbers are off before anything else is considered.

Labor and installation conditions

Pitch, height, and access all affect labor. A 10/12 roof on a two-story home is not installed at the same speed as a 4/12 ranch roof. Good scopes include steep charges, high-roof charges, and additional labor for cut-up sections with many valleys and dormers.

Interior damage

If water got inside, the scope should not stop at the shingles. Ceiling drywall, insulation, paint, and sometimes flooring belong in the same claim when the roof leak caused them.

Roofing scope of loss vs. insurance estimate vs. contractor estimate

People use these terms loosely, so it helps to separate them. The scope is the list of work. The estimate is the scope with prices attached. In practice, the carrier sends one document that does both.

A contractor's estimate is a bid to do the work. It may be a lump sum or a line-item document. Contractors often include items the carrier left out because they know what it actually takes to install the roof to manufacturer specifications and local code.

DocumentWho prepares itCommon issue
Insurance scope of lossCarrier or independent adjusterMissing items, low quantities, or wrong material
Contractor estimateRoofing contractorMay be a lump sum the carrier will not review line by line
Appraisal estimatePolicyholder's or carrier's appraiserBuilt specifically to prove the amount of loss

When the totals are far apart, the gap is almost always explained by specific missing or under-measured lines. Our guide on Xactimate vs. contractor estimates explains how to translate one format into the other.

What are the most common roofing scope of loss problems?

After reviewing many Texas roof claims, the same gaps show up again and again:

  • Missing slopes. Only the slopes facing the storm are scoped, even when the whole roof must be replaced to match.
  • Wrong pitch. An understated pitch reduces both area and labor charges.
  • No drip edge or starter. These are easy to miss and add up across a full roof.
  • Flashing left out. Step and counter flashing often cannot be reused once shingles are removed. See why flashing is commonly missed in claims.
  • Wrong material. Pricing a laminated roof as three-tab, or a Class 4 shingle as standard.
  • Low waste factor. Waste depends on roof geometry; a hip roof needs more than a simple gable.
  • No permit or code allowance. Leaves the homeowner paying for required items.
  • Interior repairs ignored. Water-stained ceilings are treated as a separate or unrelated issue.

Measurement mistakes are the root of many of these problems. Use our roof square calculator to sanity-check area, pitch, and waste before you accept a scope.

Why are insurance roof scopes sometimes incomplete?

An incomplete scope is not always bad faith. After a major hailstorm, field adjusters may handle many inspections a day. Some damage is hard to see from the ground, steep roofs can be unsafe to walk, and estimating software only includes what the adjuster enters.

Other gaps come from timing. Rotted decking, hidden flashing problems, and code items often show up only after tear-off. Interior damage may not be reported until weeks later when stains appear.

Whatever the reason, the effect is the same: a roofing scope of loss that does not cover the real cost of the repair. Our article on why insurance companies underscope roof damage goes deeper into the causes.

How should you review your roofing scope of loss?

Do not look only at the bottom line. Sit down with the scope and your contractor's estimate and work through these questions:

  1. Does the total roof area (in squares) match a measurement report or your contractor's numbers?
  2. Are all slopes included, or only some?
  3. Is the pitch correct, and are steep or high charges applied?
  4. Is the right material listed, including impact rating if you have it?
  5. Are starter, ridge cap, drip edge, and underlayment included?
  6. Are flashing, pipe jacks, vents, and other penetrations addressed?
  7. Is debris removal priced for the actual number of layers?
  8. Are permits and code-required items included?
  9. If water entered the home, are interior repairs in the scope?
Tip: Mark every line that differs between the two documents. A short list of specific missing items is far more persuasive to an adjuster than a general complaint that the estimate is "too low."

How do documentation and supplements fix a roof scope?

A supplement is a request to add items or correct quantities after the original scope is written. It is the normal way to address hidden damage and overlooked items, and most carriers expect them on roof claims.

Supplements succeed when they are backed by evidence. Match each requested item to proof:

Missing itemHelpful documentation
FlashingClose-up photos, manufacturer installation instructions, contractor notes
DeckingTear-off photos showing rot or damage, sheet counts, invoices
Interior drywallLeak photos, stain measurements, moisture readings
Code upgradeLocal code reference, permit notes, building official comments
Additional wasteRoof diagram and material calculation for complex geometry

Our claim documentation checklist helps you gather the right photos and records.

Timing matters too. Ask your contractor to photograph the decking and flashing during tear-off, before new material covers it. Once the roof is installed, that evidence is gone, and the carrier may argue an item was never needed. Send supplements in writing, keep copies of every response, and track the dates so nothing stalls.

Roof scopes, Texas storms, and the appraisal clause

Texas sees some of the most frequent and damaging hail in the country, from the Panhandle around Amarillo and Lubbock to the DFW Metroplex and Central Texas. That volume of claims puts pressure on adjusters and makes incomplete roof scopes more common.

Texas law also sets claim-handling deadlines. Under Chapter 542 of the Texas Insurance Code, insurers generally must acknowledge a claim within 15 days and accept or reject it within 15 business days after receiving the items they requested, with limited extensions. Our Texas claim deadline calculator can help you track those dates.

When the carrier agrees the roof is damaged but will not move on the amount, most Texas homeowners policies allow either side to invoke appraisal. Each side picks an appraiser, and the appraisers compare scopes line by line. If they cannot agree, an umpire decides. Texas courts have held that appraisers decide the amount of loss and can address the extent of damage, but not coverage questions. Read more in can appraisal be used for roof claims. This is general information, not legal advice.

Next steps: when to get your roof scope reviewed

Consider a professional review if you see any of these signs:

  • Your contractor's estimate is much higher than the carrier's scope.
  • Obvious components such as drip edge, flashing, or ridge cap are missing.
  • The roof area or pitch looks too low.
  • The wrong roofing material is listed.
  • Documented supplement items have been denied or ignored.
  • Interior water damage is not included.
  • You cannot replace the roof for the approved amount.

Joseph Dittman has spent his career on the policyholder side of Texas property claims, writing line-item estimates and comparing them against carrier scopes. As your appraiser, he can rebuild the roofing scope of loss from measurements and documentation and present the difference in a way the other side has to address.

faqs.q: Who writes the roofing scope of loss on an insurance claim?
faqs.a: The carrier's staff adjuster or an independent adjuster hired by the insurer usually writes the scope after inspecting the roof. It is typically built in Xactimate or Symbility. Your contractor, public adjuster, or appraiser may prepare a separate scope to compare against it and identify missing or under-measured items.

faqs.q: Can I ask my insurance company to change the roof scope?
faqs.a: Yes. You can submit a supplement request with photos, measurements, invoices, and a line-item explanation of what is missing. Insurers review supplements routinely, especially for hidden damage found during tear-off. If the carrier still disagrees on the amount, most Texas homeowners policies allow either party to invoke appraisal.

faqs.q: Why does my roof scope only include some slopes?
faqs.a: Adjusters sometimes scope only slopes that show storm damage. However, if undamaged slopes cannot be matched or repaired without harming the rest of the roof, a full replacement may be supported. Review your policy language on matching, and document discontinued materials or repairability issues to support including additional slopes.

faqs.q: Does a roofing scope of loss include interior damage?
faqs.a: It should when a covered roof leak caused the interior damage. Ceiling drywall, insulation, paint, and sometimes flooring or personal property can be part of the same claim. Report interior stains promptly, photograph them, and ask the adjuster to add those rooms to the scope rather than treating them separately.

faqs.q: What is a supplemental scope of loss?
faqs.a: A supplemental scope adds items or corrects quantities after the original estimate. Common supplement items include decking, flashing, code upgrades, extra layers of roofing, and measurement corrections. Supplements are a normal part of roof claims, and they are most successful when each added line is supported by photos or other documentation.
